blurb: Benchmarks, leaderboards, LLM judges and testing agents — and why every score needs a second look.

cards.title: The life of a benchmark

steps.p: A benchmark is a fixed set of questions with known answers, so models can be compared on equal terms.
Benchmarks get published online, and web-scale training data may then include the test questions themselves.
Once models near 100%, a benchmark stops separating them. And whatever is measured gets optimized, sometimes at the expense of real ability.

cards.aside: Treat every score as a claim to be checked, not a fact.

cards.q: MMLU, long a headline benchmark, tests…
cards.why: Broad academic knowledge. It spans law, medicine, math, history and more, about 16,000 questions. Frontier models now score near its ceiling.

cards.statement: A model with a high MMLU score is guaranteed to perform well on your specific task.
cards.why: False. Benchmarks sample narrow skills in a fixed format. Your task's data, wording and requirements may differ completely. Test on your own examples.

cards.title: A 2024 audit estimated about 6.5% of MMLU's questions contain errors — over half in its virology section.
cards.detail: The "Are We Done with MMLU?" study found wrong answer keys, ambiguous questions and multiple correct options. Near the top, models may be scored against mistakes.

cards.q: One way to detect benchmark contamination is to…
options: Ask the model if it cheated
Rephrase the questions and see whether the score drops sharply
Run it on a faster GPU
cards.why: Perturb and compare. A model that understands should handle a reworded question. A big drop suggests it memorized the originals.

cards.statement: Different labs always measure the same benchmark the same way.
cards.why: False. Prompt wording, number of examples, chain of thought and answer extraction all vary — and can move scores by several points.

cards.title: How chatbot arenas work

steps.p: A user asks a question; two anonymous models answer side by side; the user votes for the better one.
Millions of votes are turned into ratings with the Bradley–Terry model, the same idea behind chess Elo.
Model names appear only after voting, to prevent brand bias.

cards.aside: LMArena began in 2023 as Chatbot Arena, a research project from UC Berkeley's LMSYS group.

cards.q: Why are models kept anonymous until after a vote?
options: To prevent people voting based on brand rather than answer quality
cards.why: Avoiding brand bias. People tend to favor names they recognize. Blind comparison isolates the answer itself.

cards.statement: Arena rankings can be swayed by style, such as longer answers and heavy formatting.
cards.why: True. Voters often prefer longer, well-formatted replies even when content is equal. Arenas added "style control" to adjust for this.

cards.q: In an Elo-style system, beating a much higher-rated opponent earns…
options: Fewer points than beating an equal opponent
More points, because the upset was unlikely
cards.why: More points for surprises. Rating changes scale with how unexpected the result was. Beating a much weaker opponent barely moves anything.

cards.title: A 2025 paper, "The Leaderboard Illusion", alleged some labs privately tested many model variants on the arena and published only the best.
cards.detail: Picking the top score from many private tries inflates rankings. The arena's organizers disputed parts of the analysis, but the debate highlighted how leaderboards can be gamed.

cards.statement: Arena-style voting measures factual accuracy precisely.
cards.why: False. Voters judge what looks better to them in the moment and rarely verify facts. It measures preference, not correctness.

cards.title: LLM-as-a-judge

steps.p: A strong model scores outputs against a rubric, or picks the better of two answers.
It can grade thousands of open-ended answers in minutes, where human review would take weeks.
Judges favor certain positions, longer answers and outputs that resemble their own.

cards.aside: Judges work best with a clear rubric and, ideally, a reference answer.

cards.q: To correct a judge's position bias when comparing two answers, you can…
options: Run the comparison twice with the order swapped and combine results
Ask the judge to be fair
cards.why: Swap and average. If the verdict flips when the order changes, the judge was reacting to position, not quality.

cards.statement: LLM judges tend to prefer outputs written by themselves.
cards.why: True — self-preference bias. Research found models can often recognize, and favor, their own text. Using a different model family as judge helps.

cards.title: Strong LLM judges agreed with human experts about as often as humans agreed with each other.
cards.detail: The 2023 MT-Bench study found GPT-4's pairwise judgments matched human preferences over 80% of the time, similar to human-human agreement, making automated evaluation practical.

cards.q: What most improves an LLM judge's reliability?
options: A specific rubric and a reference answer to compare against
cards.why: Concrete criteria. "Is it good?" invites inconsistency. "Does it cite the right clause and stay under 100 words?" can be checked.

cards.title: Build a tiny eval for your own use
cards.body: Twenty real examples with known good answers will tell you more about a model for your work than any public leaderboard.
cards.challenge: Write down five real questions from your work with answers you trust, and run them on two AI tools.

cards.title: Beyond question-and-answer

steps.p: Agents are tested on tasks in sandboxes: fixing real bugs (SWE-bench), using desktop apps (OSWorld), or serving simulated customers.
Labs test whether models could meaningfully help with cyberattacks or biological weapons, or operate autonomously.
Frontier safety frameworks tie stronger protections to capability levels crossed in these tests.

cards.aside: Anthropic's Responsible Scaling Policy calls these levels AI Safety Levels (ASL).

cards.statement: OSWorld tests agents on real desktop applications in a virtual machine.
cards.why: True. Agents must complete tasks like editing spreadsheets or changing settings across real apps, judged by checking the final state of the computer.

cards.q: Why should agent evaluations be run many times per task?
options: Agents are stochastic, so a single run can be lucky or unlucky
cards.why: Variance. The same agent may succeed on one run and fail on the next. Reliability across repeated runs matters for real deployments.

cards.title: US and UK government AI safety institutes have tested frontier models before public release.
cards.detail: In late 2024 they jointly published pre-deployment evaluations of models including an upgraded Claude 3.5 Sonnet and OpenAI's o1, covering cyber, biological and software capabilities.

cards.statement: If a model fails a dangerous-capability test once, it definitely lacks that capability.
cards.why: False. Better prompting, tools or scaffolding can reveal abilities a simple test missed. Evaluators try hard to elicit maximum capability before concluding.

cards.q: Anthropic's Responsible Scaling Policy links safety measures to…
options: Capability thresholds a model is tested against
cards.why: Capabilities. As models cross defined thresholds, stronger security and deployment safeguards become required before release.
